title: Clamp to a Range
hints: Extending the `Comparable` protocol gives a method to every comparable type.
Clamp with `min` and `max` against the range's `lowerBound` and `upperBound`.
`func clamped(to range: ClosedRange<Self>) -> Self { min(max(self, range.lowerBound), range.upperBound) }`.
jsBridge: JS: `Math.min(Math.max(x, lo), hi)`. Swift can add `clamped(to:)` to **every** `Comparable` type with one extension (numbers, dates, strings), because protocol extensions add methods retroactively. JS would need prototype patching.

compass.q: Adding `Number.prototype.clamp` in JS is frowned upon. Why is `extension Comparable` considered fine in Swift? What makes it safer (scoping, no runtime monkey-patching)?
What happens if `low > high` when building `low...high`? Is that a compile-time or runtime error?
`ClosedRange` vs `Range` for clamping: why can't you clamp to `0..<10` as neatly?
Clamping shows up in slider values, zoom scales and scroll offsets. Where would a `Comparable` extension live in a big app, to avoid collisions?
